analysis.one_liner: Lets individuals import prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies for personal use.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2014, sent to the Senate health committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to write rules allowing Americans to buy prescription drugs from licensed Canadian pharmacies approved by the FDA and import up to a 90-day supply for their own use, with a valid U.S. prescription. It excluded controlled substances, biologics, and certain complex or fragile drugs. Patients who pay U.S. retail prices could have bought the same medicines in Canada, where government price controls keep them much cheaper.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay out of pocket for brand-name prescription drugs, especially seniors and people without adequate drug coverage, would have gained a legal route to buy the same medicines from vetted Canadian pharmacies at Canadian prices. Canadian pharmacies approved under the program would gain a new legal customer base.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required HHS to issue regulations within 180 days permitting individuals to safely import prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies in quantities up to a 90-day personal supply [S2][S3].

Only pharmacies certified as licensed in Canada, at least five years old, meeting provincial pharmacy standards, and passing FDA-approved product quality testing could be used, and HHS would publish a public list of approved pharmacies with their website addresses [S2][S3].

Imported drugs would have to have the same active ingredients, dosage form, route of administration, and strength as FDA-approved drugs, and be filled with a valid prescription from a U.S.-licensed physician [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost in reduced U.S. sales, since their products would face price competition from Canada, where government regulation holds prices far below U.S. levels. The FDA and HHS would take on the cost of certifying pharmacies and testing products.

drawbacks.text: The bill excluded controlled substances, biologics, infused and intravenous drugs, biotechnology products, refrigerated drugs, and others, so many of the newest and most expensive medicines, including most cancer biologics, could not have been imported [S3].

Opponents of drug importation have long argued it raises safety risks by moving drugs through channels outside FDA's direct control, and the FDA would have had to build a pharmacy certification and testing program to manage that risk.

Personal importation of a 90-day supply helps individuals but does not by itself lower list prices in the United States, so its benefit is limited to those able and willing to buy from an approved Canadian pharmacy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For individuals facing high U.S. drug prices, the bill offered a direct, immediate way to pay less for the same FDA-equivalent medicines, with meaningful safety conditions built in. Its reach was limited: it applied only to personal use, excluded the newest biologic drugs, and would not by itself change U.S. drug prices. The chief cost falls on drug manufacturers and on HHS, which must set up certification and testing. A well-designed but narrow cost-relief measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced S. 2549 in the Senate on June 26, 2014, joined by Sen. McCain, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The bill had three cosponsors, one Republican and two Democrats, and the committee took no further action on it; no vote was ever held before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off, because the bill never advanced far enough to expose their U.S. prices to competition from Canadian pharmacies. Americans paying high U.S. drug prices gained nothing, since importation remained illegal.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to allow personal drug importation from Canada.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alongside Klobuchar and was among its initial Republican supporters.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Tom Harkin (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action; no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: The pharmaceutical industry has historically opposed drug importation legislation, which it views as undermining its U.S. pricing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship, a Democrat from Minnesota and a Republican from Arizona leading it with a 1-R/2-D cosponsor group, but it drew too little Senate-wide support to move past committee.

industries.note: The bill would have let Americans buy the same FDA-equivalent drugs in Canada, where government controls keep prices far lower, cutting into U.S. sales and margins. The bill died in committee without a vote, so the industry kept its U.S. pricing untouched.

FDA-approved Canadian pharmacies would have gained a new legal customer base of Americans importing up to a 90-day supply, provided they met licensing, longevity, and quality-testing criteria. Their gain comes from giving patients a cheaper alternative, not from charging them more.

industries.industry: U.S. pharmacies and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: U.S. retail pharmacies would have faced some lost sales as patients shifted maintenance-drug purchases to Canada. The effect is modest because imports were capped at personal-use 90-day quantities.
